name: Pocket Anthology
desc: A small book of short poems from the Abbey shop, with a tour sheet folded inside: Wordsworth, Shakespeare and Austen, three places, one afternoon. The spine is already cracked at the daffodils.

name: The Mabinogion
desc: Eleven medieval Welsh tales in a well-thumbed paperback, a gift from the cyfarwydd at Harlech. Pwyll, Branwen, Manawydan and Math are the Four Branches; the rest is Arthur, giants and a very fast boar.

name: White Book Page
desc: A photograph of a page of the White Book of Rhydderch, about 1350, from the National Library of Wales: the opening of Branwen ferch Llŷr, with a starling the scholar drew in the margin of the copy. For the cyfarwydd at Harlech.

name: Kilmarnock Edition
desc: A facsimile of Poems, Chiefly in the Scottish Dialect, printed at Kilmarnock in 1786: Robert Burns's first book, 612 copies, three shillings each. This one was free, which he would have approved of.

name: Field Day Programme
desc: A reprint of the programme for Translations by Brian Friel, Field Day Theatre Company, the Guildhall, Derry, 23 September 1980. Stephen Rea as Owen. Somebody has written the Irish place-names back in down the margin.

name: Lemon Soap
desc: A cake of lemon soap from Sweny's chemist on Lincoln Place, wrapped in paper. Leopold Bloom bought one for fourpence on 16 June 1904 and carried it round Dublin all day in his pocket. It still smells of 1904, sweet and waxy.

name: Gorgonzola Sandwich
desc: Gorgonzola and mustard on thick bread, as served to Leopold Bloom at Davy Byrne's on Duke Street at one o'clock on Bloomsday. The glass of burgundy is not included. Restores 110 HP.

name: Straw Boater
desc: A straw boater with a black band, the Bloomsday uniform, handed on by a Joycean who had it from his father. Wear it on 16 June with a stiff collar and a pocket full of lemon soap, and quote nothing you have not read.

name: Commonplace Book
desc: A notebook for copying out lines worth keeping, begun when you had read ten plaques in Poets' Corner. The first page has a starling, a daffodil and a lemon. The rest is yours.

name: Laurel Wreath
desc: A wreath of bay leaves, the old crown of poets, for reading every arts plaque in the Gazetteer. It does not fit over a hat. Poets Laureate get a butt of sack as well; you get the wreath and the satisfaction.
